title: A Warning Amid Solomon's Success
overview: God tells Solomon that his throne and the temple depend on staying faithful, and the chapter then describes the labor, deals and wealth behind his great building projects.

parts.label: God answers Solomon (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The LORD appears to Solomon again, as in the earlier dream at Gibeon, and replies to the prayer Solomon prayed when the temple was dedicated in chapter 8. God accepts the temple as the place where his Name, meaning his presence and reputation, will dwell.

parts.label: A promise with conditions (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: If Solomon stays faithful like David, his family keeps the throne; if he or his descendants turn to other gods, Israel will lose its land and the temple will become a ruin. The book's first readers likely already knew the temple had been destroyed by Babylon, so this reads as an explanation of that disaster.

parts.label: Disappointing towns for Hiram (vv. 10-14)
parts.note: Solomon gives twenty towns in Galilee to Hiram, king of the coastal city of Tyre, as payment for timber and a vast sum of gold. Hiram is unimpressed and nicknames the area Kabul, a word whose meaning is uncertain but is often taken as "good for nothing."

parts.label: Forced labor and fortresses (vv. 15-23)
parts.note: Solomon drafted workers to build up Jerusalem and to fortify cities like Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer that guarded major roads; Gezer had been burned by Egypt's king and given as a wedding gift. Descendants of the land's earlier peoples were made permanent slaves while Israelites served as soldiers and overseers, though other passages (5:13; 12:4) show Israelites also bore heavy labor.

parts.label: Palace and festivals (vv. 24-25)
parts.note: Solomon's Egyptian wife moves into the palace he built for her. Solomon offers sacrifices at the three main yearly festivals, keeping the temple's regular worship going.

parts.label: Ships bring gold (vv. 26-28)
parts.note: Solomon builds a fleet at a port on the Red Sea, crewed partly by Hiram's skilled sailors, and it returns with huge amounts of gold from Ophir. No one knows for sure where Ophir was; suggestions include Arabia, East Africa and India.

disagreement: Christians differ on how this conditional warning fits with God's earlier promise that David's family would rule forever: some see the promise as broken by Israel's unfaithfulness, while others read it as ultimately kept in Jesus, whom Christians see as David's lasting heir.
think: When something impressive gets built, whether a nation, a business or a reputation, what do you think actually keeps it standing over time?
